title: Cycle Detection in Directed & Undirected Graphs
summary: Detecting a cycle needs genuinely different bookkeeping depending on whether the graph is directed or undirected — reusing one graph type's trick on the other silently produces wrong answers.

slides.markdown:
"Does this graph have a cycle" sounds like one question, but it needs two genuinely different algorithms depending on whether the graph is directed or undirected — the naive "have I seen this node before" check that works for undirected graphs gives **false positives** on directed ones.

Undirected cycle detection needs to remember where you came from (the parent). Directed cycle detection needs to remember your entire current path, not just your immediate predecessor — the three-color method. Confusing the two is one of the most common graph-algorithm bugs in interviews, because both "look like" the same DFS at a glance.

slides.sectionTitle: Undirected: a visited neighbor that isn't your parent
slides.markdown:
In an undirected graph, every edge is stored both ways: if `u-v` is an edge, DFS from `u` will immediately see `v` as a neighbor, and DFS from `v` will immediately see `u` back. That means the edge you just came from will *always* appear as an already-visited neighbor — that's not a cycle, it's just the edge doubling back on itself.

The fix: track the parent you arrived from, and only treat a visited neighbor as a real cycle if it is **not** that parent. Any other already-visited neighbor genuinely means you've found a second path back to a node you've seen before — a cycle.

slides.sectionTitle: DFS cycle check for undirected graphs

slides.markdown:
In a directed graph, edges only go one way, so the parent trick doesn't apply — there's no "edge doubling back" to filter out, because a directed edge `u → v` doesn't imply `v → u` exists at all. But a plain "have I visited this node before, anywhere in the whole traversal" check is *too* strict: it flags a node as a cycle even when it was reached via a completely separate, finished branch, not the current path.

What actually matters is: is this node on my **current recursion path** right now, or was it visited and *already fully finished* on some earlier, unrelated branch? Those are very different situations, and directed cycle detection needs to distinguish them.

Give every node one of three states: **white** (unvisited), **gray** (currently on the recursion stack — in progress), **black** (fully finished, every descendant explored). A node becomes gray when DFS enters it, and only becomes black when DFS is completely done with it and all its descendants.

A cycle exists exactly when DFS encounters an edge pointing to a **gray** node — that's a back edge into the current path, meaning you can walk from that gray node back to itself. An edge to a black node is fine: it means you've reached an already-fully-explored, unrelated part of the graph, not a cycle back into your current path.

slides.sectionTitle: DFS cycle check for directed graphs

slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a directed graph DFS tree with a root and two branches; on one branch, draw a dashed arrow from a deep descendant back up to one of its own ancestors, labelled "back edge — creates a cycle"; on the other branch, draw a dashed arrow from a node in one branch sideways to an already-finished (black) node in a different, unrelated branch, labelled "cross edge — no cycle" >>>

Only the back edge — pointing to a node still gray, still on the current path — signals a cycle. The cross edge points to a node that's already black, fully finished and unrelated to the current path, and is completely normal in a directed graph with no cycle at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Union-Find as a second undirected cycle detector
slides.markdown:
Union-Find gives a second, non-DFS way to detect a cycle in an **undirected** graph while building it edge by edge: before unioning two nodes, check if they're already in the same set. If they are, this edge closes a cycle; if not, union them.

This only works cleanly for undirected graphs — Union-Find has no notion of edge direction, so it can't distinguish a directed back edge from a directed cross edge the way the three-color method does. For directed cycle detection, DFS with the three-color method (or the topological-sort-based check below) is the standard approach.

| | Parent-tracking DFS | Union-Find |
|---|---|---|
| Graph type | Undirected only | Undirected only |
| When all edges known upfront | O(V+E), one pass | O(E · α(V)) ≈ O(E) |
| Edges arriving incrementally | Needs a fresh traversal per check | O(α(V)) per check, no re-traversal |
| Extra info from the same pass | Can also produce a topological-adjacent traversal order | Only connectivity, no ordering |

Same offline-vs-online distinction as connected components: if you're checking for a cycle once, over a graph you already have in full, either works and DFS is often simpler to reach for. If edges are streaming in and you need to know the instant a cycle forms, Union-Find's incremental check is the better fit.

A **directed** graph has a valid topological order if and only if it has no cycle — a cycle means some set of nodes each depend on each other, so there's no way to linearly order them all with every dependency coming first.

This gives a third way to detect a directed cycle: run Kahn's algorithm (repeatedly removing zero-in-degree nodes). If every node eventually gets removed, there's no cycle. If some nodes are **left over** — never reaching zero in-degree because they're stuck in a mutual dependency — those leftover nodes are exactly the cycle. This connection is covered in full in the topological-sort topic.

slides.sectionTitle: The two mistakes that swap between graph types
slides.markdown:
Two mirrored bugs, each from applying the wrong graph type's trick:

- **Reusing the undirected "skip the parent" rule on a directed graph.** Directed edges don't double back the way undirected ones do, so there's no parent edge to skip — you need the gray/black distinction instead, and "skip the immediate predecessor" doesn't generalize to directed graphs at all.
- **Treating any revisited node as a cycle, on a directed graph, instead of checking if it's still on the current path (gray).** A node visited and fully finished on an earlier, unrelated branch (black) is not a cycle — only a node still in progress on the current path (gray) is. Skipping the color distinction and using plain "seen before" produces false positives on any DAG with a node reachable via two different paths, which is an extremely common, entirely valid shape.
